items.q: What does this print, and why is it a classic bug?
items.code:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add(1))
print(add(2))
items.a_short: `[1]` then `[1, 2]` — the default list is created once, at function definition time, and shared across every call.
items.a_full: Default arguments are evaluated once when the `def` statement executes, not on each call. The fix is `def add(item, bucket=None)` then `if bucket is None: bucket = []` inside the body.

items.a_short: `[[1], [1], [1]]` — all three slots reference the same list object.
items.a_full: `*` on a list copies references, not objects. Use `[[] for _ in range(3)]` to get three independent lists.

items.q: `is` vs `==` — what does each actually compare?
items.a_short: `is` compares identity (same object in memory); `==` compares value via `__eq__`.
items.a_full: Use `is` only for singletons: `None`, `True`, `False`, sentinel objects. Small ints (-5 to 256) and some short strings are interned, so `a is b` can be accidentally True for them — never rely on that.

items.a_short: Name lookup order: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in.
items.a_full: Python searches the local function scope first, then any enclosing function scopes, then module globals, then builtins. `global` rebinds at module level; `nonlocal` rebinds in the nearest enclosing function scope.

items.code:
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])
items.a_short: `[2, 2, 2]` — closures capture the variable, not its value at creation time.
items.a_full: By the time the lambdas run, the loop has finished and `i` is 2. Bind it eagerly with a default argument: `lambda i=i: i`.

items.q: Generator expression vs list comprehension — when does the difference matter?
items.a_short: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory; a generator yields one item at a time and holds O(1) state.
items.a_full: Use a generator for large or infinite streams, or when you only iterate once. Use a list when you need indexing, `len()`, or multiple passes. A generator is consumed once — iterating it again yields nothing.

options: Generators are lazy and O(1) memory; lists are eager and O(n)
Lists are lazy, generators are eager

items.code:
g = (x * x for x in range(4))
print(sum(g))
print(sum(g))
items.a_short: `14` then `0` — the generator is exhausted after the first pass.
items.a_full: Generators are single-use iterators. Once consumed they raise `StopIteration` immediately, so `sum` over an exhausted generator returns 0.

items.a_short: A callable that takes a function and returns a replacement. `@dec` above `def f` is sugar for `f = dec(f)`.
items.a_full: Decorators with arguments need a third layer: the outer call returns the actual decorator. Always apply `functools.wraps` to the wrapper so `__name__`, `__doc__` and `__wrapped__` survive.

options: A class that wraps a function
A callable returning a replacement callable; `@d` means `f = d(f)`

items.q: Why is `functools.wraps` needed on a decorator's wrapper?
items.a_short: Without it the wrapper's own `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__module__` and signature shadow the original function's.
items.a_full: That breaks introspection, debuggers, documentation tools and anything relying on `help()`. `wraps` also sets `__wrapped__`, which lets `inspect.signature` dig through to the real function.

options: It preserves the wrapped function's metadata

items.q: What is the GIL and what does it actually prevent?
items.a_short: A single mutex in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time — so threads give no CPU-bound speedup.
items.a_full: I/O-bound work still benefits from threads because the GIL is released during blocking I/O, and C extensions (NumPy, PyTorch) release it during heavy compute. For CPU-bound Python, use `multiprocessing` or move the hot loop into C/NumPy.

options: It allows only one thread to run Python bytecode at a time
It blocks all I/O during compute

items.q: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio — which for what?
items.a_short: threading for blocking I/O, multiprocessing for CPU-bound work, asyncio for very high-concurrency non-blocking I/O.
items.a_full: Threads share memory (cheap data sharing, needs locks). Processes have separate memory (true parallelism, pickling overhead at the boundary). asyncio is single-threaded cooperative scheduling — thousands of sockets, but one blocking call stalls the whole loop.

options: threading for CPU, multiprocessing for I/O
threading for I/O, multiprocessing for CPU, asyncio for high-concurrency I/O

items.a_short: Shallow copies the outer container but shares the nested objects; deep recursively copies everything.
items.a_full: `list(x)`, `x[:]` and `copy.copy(x)` are shallow. `copy.deepcopy(x)` walks the object graph and handles cycles via a memo dict — correct but slow.
items.code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3]]
b = copy.copy(a)
b[0].append(99)
print(a)

items.q: list vs tuple — beyond mutability, what changes?
items.a_short: Tuples are hashable (usable as dict keys / set members), slightly smaller and faster to construct, and signal fixed structure.
items.a_full: A tuple is only hashable if everything inside it is. Lists have extra capacity for amortized O(1) append, which costs memory; tuples are allocated exactly.

options: Tuples are hashable, more compact, and fixed-structure

items.a_short: Yes — insertion order is an implementation detail in 3.6 and a language guarantee from 3.7 onward.
items.a_full: The compact dict layout stores entries in a dense insertion-ordered array with a sparse index table, which cut memory ~20% and gave ordering for free. `collections.OrderedDict` still differs: it has `move_to_end` and order-sensitive `==`.

items.q: Average-case complexity of `x in list`, `x in set`, `x in dict`?
items.a_short: List is O(n); set and dict are O(1) average, O(n) worst case under hash collisions.
items.a_full: Converting a list to a set before repeated membership tests turns an O(n·m) loop into O(n+m) — one of the highest-value one-line optimizations in interview coding rounds.

items.q: Why is `''.join(parts)` preferred over repeated `s += x` in a loop?
items.a_short: Strings are immutable, so each `+=` allocates a new string and copies — O(n²) overall. `join` sizes the buffer once and copies once.
items.a_full: CPython has an in-place optimization when a string has refcount 1, which sometimes hides the cost, but it is not guaranteed and vanishes the moment another reference exists.

options: += is O(n²) because strings are immutable; join is O(n)
join uses less memory but is slower

items.a_short: `fdb` then an empty string.
items.a_full: A negative step walks backwards from the end. Out-of-range slices clamp silently and return empty — unlike indexing, which raises `IndexError`.

items.q: Iterable vs iterator — what's the distinction?
items.a_short: An iterable implements `__iter__`; an iterator implements both `__iter__` and `__next__` and carries position state.
items.a_full: `iter(iterable)` returns a fresh iterator. A list is iterable but not an iterator — that's why you can loop over a list many times but a generator only once.

options: Iterable has __iter__; iterator has __iter__ and __next__ plus state

items.q: How does `with` work under the hood?
items.a_short: The object's `__enter__` runs on entry; `__exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)` runs on exit, even if an exception was raised.
items.a_full: Returning a truthy value from `__exit__` suppresses the exception. `contextlib.contextmanager` lets you write one with a generator: code before `yield` is enter, after is exit, and a `try/finally` guarantees cleanup.

options: Calls __enter__ on entry and __exit__ on exit, including on exceptions

items.a_short: `finally` then `try` — the `finally` block runs before the function actually returns.
items.a_full: The return value is evaluated and stashed, `finally` executes, then the value is returned. A `return` inside `finally` would overwrite it, which is why that is a lint error in most codebases.

items.q: What does the `else` clause on a `try` block do?
items.a_short: It runs only if no exception was raised, before `finally`.
items.a_full: It keeps the `try` body down to just the line that can fail, so you don't accidentally catch exceptions from follow-up code that was never meant to be guarded.

options: Runs only when no exception was raised

items.a_short: Reference counting frees objects immediately at count zero; a generational cycle collector handles reference cycles.
items.a_full: Three generations; an object surviving a collection is promoted. Cycles containing objects with `__del__` were uncollectable before 3.4. `gc.disable()` is sometimes a real win in short-lived batch jobs.

options: Reference counting plus a generational cycle collector

items.a_short: `False` then `True` — binary floating point can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly.
items.a_full: Compare floats with `math.isclose(a, b)` or an explicit tolerance. Use `decimal.Decimal` for money, `fractions.Fraction` for exact rationals.

items.a_short: Code that should run only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported.
items.a_full: On import, `__name__` is the module's name; when run as a script it is `'__main__'`. This matters a lot with `multiprocessing` on Windows and macOS spawn, where child processes re-import the main module.

options: Code that runs only when the file is executed directly

items.a_short: `[1, 3]` — but only by luck. Removing while iterating shifts elements under the loop's internal index, so an element gets skipped.
items.a_full: Trace it: at index 1 the loop sees 2 and removes it, so the list becomes [1,3,4] and 3 slides into index 1 — already passed. The loop moves to index 2, sees 4, removes it. The skipped element happened to be odd, so the answer looks right. Change the input to [1,2,4,3] and it breaks. Never mutate a list you are iterating: `nums = [n for n in nums if n % 2]`.

items.q: Is Python's `sorted` stable, and what algorithm does it use?
items.a_short: Yes, stable — equal elements keep their original relative order. It uses Timsort, O(n log n) worst case, O(n) on nearly-sorted input.
items.a_full: Stability lets you sort by multiple keys in passes: sort by the secondary key first, then by the primary. Or do it in one go with a tuple key: `key=lambda r: (r.dept, -r.score)`.

items.a_short: `global` binds a name at module level; `nonlocal` binds it in the nearest enclosing function scope.
items.a_full: Without either, assigning to a name inside a function makes it local for the entire function body — which is why reading it before assignment raises `UnboundLocalError` rather than falling back to the outer scope.

options: global → module scope, nonlocal → nearest enclosing function scope
global works only at class level

items.code:
x = 10
def f():
    print(x)
    x = 5
f()
items.a_short: `UnboundLocalError` — the assignment makes `x` local for the whole function, so the `print` reads an unbound local.
items.a_full: Python decides local-vs-global at compile time by scanning for assignments, not at runtime line by line. Add `global x` if you really mean the module-level name.

items.a_short: `enumerate` gives index+value without a counter, `zip` walks sequences in lockstep and stops at the shortest, `any`/`all` short-circuit.
items.a_full: `zip(*matrix)` transposes. `zip(strict=True)` (3.10+) raises if lengths differ, catching silent truncation. `any`/`all` over a generator stop as soon as the result is decided.

options: zip stops at the shortest and any/all short-circuit

items.code:
vals = [0, '', [], None, 'False', 0.0, {}]
print(sum(1 for v in vals if v))
items.a_short: `1` — only the non-empty string `'False'` is truthy.
items.a_full: Falsy values: `False`, `None`, zero of any numeric type, and empty containers/strings. A non-empty string is always truthy no matter what it spells.

items.q: What does the walrus operator `:=` do?
items.a_short: Assigns a value as part of an expression, so you can bind and test in one step.
items.a_full: Common uses: `while (chunk := f.read(8192)):` and `if (m := re.search(p, s)):`. It keeps the value in scope without a pre-loop read or duplicated call.

items.a_short: `append(x)` adds one element; `extend(it)` adds each element of an iterable; `+=` on a list behaves like `extend` and mutates in place.
items.a_full: `lst = lst + other` creates a new list and rebinds; `lst += other` mutates the original, which is visible to every other reference to it. That difference bites when the list is a function argument.
items.code:
a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
b = [1, 2]
b.extend([3, 4])
print(a, b)

items.q: A Python function is too slow. What's your order of attack?
items.a_short: Measure first (`cProfile`, `line_profiler`), fix algorithmic complexity, then vectorize with NumPy, then cache, then drop to C/Cython/Numba.
items.a_full: Never optimize on intuition — the hot line is almost never where you'd guess. Big wins in order: better data structure (set/dict lookups), removing work from inner loops, `functools.lru_cache` on pure functions, NumPy to move loops into C, and only then a native extension.

options: Profile, fix complexity, vectorize, cache, then go native

items.a_short: `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from the annotated class attributes.
items.a_full: `frozen=True` makes instances immutable and hashable; `slots=True` (3.10+) cuts per-instance memory by dropping `__dict__`; `field(default_factory=list)` is the safe way to default a mutable attribute.
